NOT the unsourced '8 m framed hall' claim.<br>`width_min`: cruck dwelling <=6 m (buildingconservation.com, timber-framed buildings) — lower bound of the framed range<br>`bays`: DESIGN DECISION (analogy, not an inn measurement): modelled on the grounded hall_house 4-bay frame, inn ground floor ~= a hall. Taproom = the 2 middle bays (cf. hall_house open hall = middle 2 bays, Wikipedia Hall house); kitchen + store one bay each. No inn-specific bay count was sourced.<br>`bay_length`: ~4 m timber-frame bay module shared with croft/longhouse/hall_house (DERIVED; same Brunskill 1985 TBD caveat as those entries)<br>`stories`: 2 storeys: ground-floor public rooms + upper-floor guest chambers — the standard town-inn lodging form. Attested: The New Inn, Gloucester is a three-storey galleried inn with chambers on the upper floors (Wikipedia). 2 is the conservative town-tavern default; multi-story gen supports more. (Medievalists.net grounds the inn room programme — hall/chambers/kitchen — but not the vertical placement.)<br>`example_for_TYPE_only`: The New Inn, Gloucester (timber-framed galleried courtyard inn, c.1430-50, ~40 chambers; Wikipedia) attests medieval inns as multi-storey galleried buildings with many guest chambers — evidence for the TYPE + the upstairs-lodging direction, NOT for this 4-bay scale (it is a large 7-bay courtyard inn). |
